text: Hana had been sure she had left the gas on when she rushed out that morning. All through the bus ride home she pictured the flat full of fumes, the neighbors, the fire engines. She ran up the stairs and burst into the kitchen, and every knob on the stove was turned firmly off. The room smelled only of toast. Hana leaned against the counter and let out a long, shaky breath, and felt her shoulders drop from around her ears. Her legs went a little weak. She laughed out loud at nothing, put the kettle on, and sank into a chair.

Milo's dinner guests were due in ten minutes and he was certain the roast was ruined; the kitchen smelled of smoke and he had forgotten the timer. He yanked open the oven. The smoke was only from a drip of fat on the oven floor. The roast itself sat golden and perfect, the thermometer reading exactly right. Milo let out a breath he had been holding for an hour. The tightness in his chest unwound all at once. He sagged against the counter, grinning, and when the doorbell rang he went to answer it with his whole body loose and light.

Esme's train had stopped in a tunnel for forty minutes, and her job interview was at nine. She had sat rigid, watching the minutes tick past. Then a message came: the interviewer's own train was stuck too, and the meeting was moved to the afternoon. Esme read it three times. The knot in her stomach loosened, and her shoulders, which had been up near her ears, finally came down. She slumped back into the seat and closed her eyes, letting out a long breath. The rest of the delay no longer mattered. She almost laughed out loud.

Driving to work, Gus heard a loud bang from the engine and saw smoke, and his heart sank; he could not afford another repair. He pulled onto the shoulder and opened the bonnet. It was only a split hose, a cheap part, and a passing mechanic taped it for him in five minutes and refused any money. Gus stood by the road with oily hands and felt the weight lift off him. His breath came out in a long whoosh. He thanked the man three times, got back in the car, and sat for a moment with his hands loose on the wheel, grinning at the windscreen.

Kai's father had gone into surgery at eight in the morning, and by four there had been no word. Kai sat by the phone, unable to eat, going through every possibility. At half past four it rang. His sister's voice: it went well, he is awake, he asked for tea. Kai sank back into the sofa, his whole body going slack. His eyes stung. The breath went out of him in a long, shaking rush, and for a moment he could not speak at all. Then he laughed, and asked her to say it again, just to hear it.

Una had not heard from her daughter, traveling abroad, for three days, and the news was full of the storm there. She had barely slept. Then, at breakfast, her phone buzzed with a video call, and there was her daughter's face, sunburned and grinning, saying the phone had fallen in the sea. Una put her hand over her heart and felt it slow. Every muscle in her body let go at once. She sat down heavily on the kitchen chair, laughing and shaking her head, her eyes wet, and asked her to turn the camera around so she could see the whole room.

Pia had deleted the entire client database by mistake at five o'clock, and for two hours had sat sweating while the technician searched. Her career, she was sure, was over. Then he leaned back and said the backup from that morning was complete; nothing was lost. Pia's whole body sagged. She let out a breath she seemed to have been holding since five. Her hands stopped trembling. She laughed, too loudly, and thanked him over and over, and then put her head down on the desk and stayed there, just breathing, feeling the tension drain out of her neck.

The layoffs were announced by email at noon, and Bram sat staring at the unopened message, his stomach tight. Half his team had already been called in. He clicked. His name was on the list of roles that would stay. He read it twice to be sure. The tightness in his chest let go, and he slumped back in his chair, his arms loose at his sides. He breathed out slowly through his mouth. The office noise, which had seemed so sharp all morning, softened to a hum. For the first time in weeks, his shoulders stopped aching.

Pia had watched the storm all night from her window, sure it would flatten the greenhouse and the seedlings she had raised since February. At dawn she went out in her boots through the wet grass, bracing herself. The greenhouse stood. Not a pane was cracked. Inside, the seedlings sat in their trays, dry and green and upright. Pia leaned against the doorframe and let out a long breath, and felt her shoulders loosen. She laughed a little at herself. She stood there for a while in the warm damp air, smelling the soil, her body heavy and easy.

Lior had been told the old oak in his garden would have to come down, the roots were rotten, and it would cost more than he had. Today a second tree surgeon climbed it, tapped it, dug around its base, and came down smiling. The tree was sound; the first man had been wrong. Lior felt the tightness in his chest loosen all at once. He put his hand on the rough bark and let his breath out slowly. His knees felt a little unsteady. He sat down on the bench beneath the branches and simply sat, looking up at the leaves.

For a week Vera had waited for the scan results, imagining the worst. Now the doctor looked up from the screen and smiled. It was a cyst, harmless, nothing to do. Vera heard the words and felt her whole body unclench, from her jaw to her toes. Her breath came out in a rush. She put her hand to her mouth. The room seemed suddenly brighter, the poster on the wall almost funny. Outside in the car park she sat in the car for ten minutes without starting it, laughing quietly and wiping her eyes.

Femi had carried his son into the clinic at midnight, burning with fever and limp, and waited while they ran tests. At two the doctor came out: an ordinary virus, nothing serious; the fever would pass. Femi's legs went weak and he sat down hard on the plastic chair. His breath shuddered out of him. The tightness he had carried in his chest for hours let go all at once, and he felt suddenly exhausted, heavy and light at the same time. When they brought his son out, sleepy and cooler, he held him and did not want to put him down.

The envelope from the tax office had sat on Noor's table all morning, unopened, while she imagined the fine, the audit, the debt. At last she tore it open. It was a refund: two hundred back, for an overpayment she had not noticed. Noor read it twice, and then her shoulders dropped and she let out a long breath that turned into a laugh. The tightness behind her eyes eased. She propped the letter against the fruit bowl and made herself a proper breakfast, humming, her whole body loose for the first time in days.

Ivo's passport had not arrived, and his flight was the next morning. He had called the office six times. Then, at five in the afternoon, the doorbell rang and a courier handed him a stiff envelope. Inside was the passport, his tired face staring up from the photo page. Ivo leaned against the doorframe, the breath leaving him in a long rush. His hands, which had been clenched all day, opened. He laughed at nothing. He went inside, put the passport in the front pocket of his bag, zipped it, and lay down on the sofa, heavy and loose.

Zola's cat had been missing for four days, and she had checked every shed and alley in the neighborhood. On the fifth morning she opened the back door and there he was on the step, thin and dusty, meowing crossly for breakfast. Zola sank down onto the step beside him. Her breath came out in a long shudder. She gathered him onto her lap and felt his warm weight and the rumble of his purr, and the tightness she had carried in her chest all week melted away. She sat there in her dressing gown, stroking him, in no hurry at all.

The vet had kept Jun's old dog overnight after he swallowed a sock, and warned that surgery might be needed. Jun had not slept. In the morning the vet called: the sock had passed on its own; the dog was fine and could go home. Jun sat down on the stairs with the phone still at his ear. His whole body went slack. He breathed out slowly, and the pressure behind his eyes eased. When he picked the dog up an hour later and it licked his face, wagging, Jun laughed, a long, loose, tired laugh, and held it close.

The sale of Tavi's old flat had fallen through twice, and if it failed again she would lose the new place too. All week she had carried the tension in her jaw. On Friday afternoon the agent called: contracts exchanged, it was done. Tavi sat down on a packing box in the empty living room and let her head fall back against the wall. The breath went out of her in a long sigh. Her shoulders dropped. She stayed there, among the boxes, feeling the whole week drain out of her body, a slow smile spreading across her face.

Eli had been told the moving truck with everything he owned had been in an accident on the motorway. For two hours he could get no details. Then the company called back: the truck had been hit from behind, but the cargo was untouched, and it would arrive tomorrow. Eli sank onto the bare floor of his new flat and let out a breath that seemed to go on forever. His hands stopped shaking. He lay back on the floorboards, staring at the ceiling, and laughed quietly, his whole body going slack and heavy.

Wren was cycling home when her front wheel hit a pothole and she went flying over the handlebars toward the traffic. She landed on the grass verge, rolled, and lay still for a moment, taking stock. Nothing hurt too badly. She moved her arms, her legs. Just a scraped palm. The bicycle was barely bent. Wren lay on her back on the cool grass, looking up at the sky, and let out a long breath. Her heart slowed. She started to laugh, lying there, her body heavy and loose, the grass soft against her neck.

Amir had lost his wallet somewhere on his long bicycle ride, with his cards, his cash, and the only photograph of his late mother. He retraced the whole route in the dusk, searching the verges. At the last bend a woman was waiting by the gate of a farmhouse, holding it up. She had found it by the road; nothing was missing. Amir took it and opened it, and there was the photograph. His whole body went soft. The breath went out of him in a long sigh, and he thanked her again and again, grinning, his legs suddenly shaky.

In the crowded market Hana lost sight of her small son for three long minutes. She had pushed through the crowds calling his name, her heart hammering. Then she saw him, sitting on an upturned crate at the fruit stall, eating a free strawberry, chatting happily with the old woman who ran it. Hana's legs nearly gave way. She scooped him up and held him tight, her breath coming out in a long shudder, and felt her whole body unwind. The old woman smiled. Hana laughed, shakily, and bought far more strawberries than they needed.

At the market checkout Teo reached for his wallet and found his pocket empty; he was sure it had been stolen, with his whole week's wages inside. He had searched every pocket twice, his face hot. Then the stall holder called out: a boy had handed it in, and there it was, on the shelf behind the till, everything still inside. Teo let out a long breath. The tightness drained from his shoulders. He laughed and shook the man's hand and pressed a note into it, and walked home slowly through the stalls, feeling light and loose.

The rain had been pouring for hours, and Cleo's teenage daughter, out on her bicycle, was not answering her phone. Cleo stood at the window watching the flooded street, her stomach clenched. At last, at six, the gate clicked, and her daughter came up the path, soaked to the skin and grinning, her phone dead in her pocket. Cleo opened the door and felt the tension drain from her whole body at once. Her breath went out in a sigh. She wrapped her daughter in a towel and held her, laughing, and put the kettle on.

All afternoon, stuck indoors by the rain, Sami had been sure he had lost the only copy of his thesis; the laptop had died and would not start. He had searched every folder and every drive. Then, in the last email account he checked, there it was: a copy he had sent himself a week ago, almost complete. Sami pushed his chair back from the desk and let out a long breath. His shoulders dropped. He closed his eyes and felt the whole tight afternoon leave his body, and sat there listening to the rain, smiling.

Nell's friend had been due for dinner at seven and had not come or called, and Nell had spent an hour imagining accidents. At half past eight the doorbell rang, and there she was, holding a cake, explaining that her phone had died and her train had broken down. Nell hugged her in the doorway, and felt the tightness in her chest let go. She breathed out slowly. Her friend was fine. Everything was fine. She laughed and took the cake and pulled her inside, and the evening, which had felt so tight, opened out easily around them.

Quin had lent his old friend a large sum of money a year ago and had begun to think he would never see it again, or the friend either. Then the friend came to visit, sat down at the kitchen table, and slid an envelope across: every penny, with a note of thanks. Quin felt a knot he had not even noticed loosen in his stomach. He let out a long breath and laughed. The friendship was intact. They sat talking late into the evening, and Quin felt his whole body easy and heavy in the chair.

The mechanic had said Rhea's old car probably needed a new engine, which she could not afford. She sat in the waiting room for two hours, her stomach in knots. Then he came out wiping his hands: it was only a loose wire, fixed now, no charge for the diagnosis. Rhea's shoulders dropped. She breathed out slowly, and felt the tightness leave her jaw. She drove home with the windows down, the old engine humming, and noticed for the first time all week how the evening light fell across the fields.

Tavi had bumped a car at the lights in his old hatchback and was sure it would cost him a fortune. He got out, shaking. The other driver, an elderly man, walked around the back of his car, bent down, and straightened up with a shrug. Not a scratch on either car; the bumpers had just kissed. The man waved and drove off. Tavi stood in the road and let out a long breath, and felt his whole body unclench. He got back in the car, sat for a moment with his hands in his lap, and laughed quietly.

Bea arrived at school pickup twenty minutes late, her heart racing, sure her son would be alone on the steps. Instead he was in the library corner with the teacher, deep in a story, and barely looked up when she came in. He had not noticed the time at all. Bea felt the tightness in her chest release. She leaned against the doorframe and let out a long breath, watching him turn the page. Her shoulders came down. When he finally ran to her, she held him longer than usual, smiling into his hair.

The school had called Rafa to say his daughter had hit her head in the playground and he should come at once. He drove there with his heart in his throat. When he rushed into the office, she was sitting on a chair with an ice pack, swinging her legs, and said, hello, Dad, I got a sticker. Just a bump; the nurse had checked. Rafa's whole body went slack. He let out a breath that shook. He knelt and hugged her, laughing, and felt the tension of the drive melt out of his arms and shoulders.

Yara's son had swum out too far at the lake, and for a long moment she lost sight of his head among the waves. She was already running into the water when she saw him, waving from the floating raft, perfectly fine, grinning. Yara stopped knee-deep in the lake. Her breath came out in a long shudder and her legs went weak. She stood there with the water lapping around her, laughing and shaking her head, feeling her whole body loosen, until he swam back and she wrapped him in a towel.

Zeb had dropped his wedding ring off the jetty into the lake and spent an hour diving for it in the murky water. He had given up. Then, on the last dive, his fingers closed on something small and hard in the silt. He burst up into the air and opened his hand: the ring. Zeb floated on his back in the water, the ring clenched in his fist, and let out a long breath. His whole body went loose. He lay there under the open sky, laughing, letting the water hold him up, feeling the whole hour of searching drain away.
